items.content_html:
Summary

Fixes #48787.

When calling logger.tagged(*tags) without a block, ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging returns a new logger with the tags applied as instance/local tags.

Previously, LocalTagStorage implemented this by defining attr_accessor :tag_stack on the formatter instance, storing tags in an instance variable (@tag_stack = TagStack.new). Because @tag_stack was an instance variable on the formatter rather than stored in IsolatedExecutionState, it was shared across all threads using that formatter. Consequently:

  • Any block-scoped tagging (e.g. logger.tagged("Job") { ... }) on such a logger mutated the shared @tag_stack, causing tags from one thread to leak into concurrent threads or nested threads.
  • push_tags, pop_tags, and clear_tags! operations on the logger mutated the shared instance variable across threads.
  • Cloned formatters inherited the memoized @thread_key from the original formatter, causing different formatters to share execution state.

Solution

  1. In LocalTagStorage, store instance-level tags separately in @local_tags (precomputing @local_tags_string for fast formatting) instead of replacing tag_stack.
  2. Keep tag_stack backed by IsolatedExecutionState, ensuring that all dynamic/block-scoped tagging and push/pop operations remain isolated per thread/fiber.
  3. Update Formatter#call and Formatter#tags_text to format both @local_tags and tag_stack.tags.
  4. Reset @thread_key = nil in Formatter#initialize_clone and Formatter#initialize_dup so cloned formatters receive distinct execution state keys.
  5. In TaggedLogging#initialize_clone and TaggedLogging#initialize_dup, ensure the formatter is also cloned/duped.
items.title: Fix thread isolation for TaggedLogging instances created without block

items.content_html:
Summary

Fixes #42802.

Integer division of a duration (e.g. 1.hour / 10) truncates parts to integers, and zero parts are dropped during initialization. That leaves a duration with an empty parts hash but a non-zero value (360 seconds). When such a duration is added to another, the merge logic only looked at parts, so those seconds were lost from both parts and inspect output.

This change treats empty parts as { seconds: value } when merging durations in Duration#+, Duration::Scalar#+, and Duration::Scalar#-.

Before / After

(1.second + 1.hour / 10).inspect
# Before: "1 second"
# After:  "361 seconds"

(1.second + 1.hour / 10).parts
# Before: { seconds: 1 }
# After:  { seconds: 361 }

Test plan

  • Repro script: ruby -I../rails/activesupport/lib duration_inspect_42802_test.rb
  • cd activesupport && bin/test test/core_ext/duration_test.rb (86 runs, 0 failures)
items.title: Fix #42802: Duration#inspect after integer division

items.content_html:
The change removes two outdated paragraphs from the Active Support core extensions guide that still promised a DateTime fallback for out-of-range Time values.

The fallback was removed from Time#change in July 2012 (98b46bf), when it stopped delegating to Time.utc_time/Time.local_time and started constructing Time directly. Time#since and Time#ago kept a bare rescue fallback to to_datetime until it was narrowed to rescue TypeError in July 2024 (efd0e6c, #52370) and removed entirely in October 2025 (a855714).

The underlying Time.time_with_datetime_fallback, Time.utc_time, and Time.local_time were deprecated in December 2012 (48583f8) and removed in July 2013 (ec5e03b).

items.content_html:
Deals with errors such as @serialize_cast_value_compatible from ActiveRecord::Type::DateTime

serialize_cast_value_compatible? memoizes into a class ivar. The eager compute in #initialize normally keeps that write on main, but ActiveRecord::Type::TypeMap builds types lazily, so a column first touched inside a Ractor raises straight out of #initialize. The other reacher, .serialize, has an inline rescue nil that swallows the IsolationError and leaves the type on #serialize for the rest of the process.

This proxies only the first write through ActiveSupport::Ractors.on_main, keeping the defined? read as the fast path: false is a legitimate memo value, so the guard cannot become ||=. Three tests, all failing without it.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #57822.

Mailgun inbound email webhooks send the entire raw RFC 822 email payload (including attachments) in a URL-encoded form parameter named body-mime with Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded.

In Rack 3, Rack::QueryParser enforces a default bytesize_limit of 4 MB (4194304 bytes). When an incoming email exceeds 4 MB, Rack raises Rack::QueryParser::QueryLimitError, which Rails converts into ActionController::BadRequest. The request is rejected before Action Mailbox can process the email.

Detail

This Pull Request resolves the issue by introducing a scoped request parser middleware specifically for the Mailgun ingress:

  1. ActionMailbox::Ingresses::Mailgun::RequestParser:

    • Only intercepts POST requests to /rails/action_mailbox/mailgun/inbound_emails/mime with application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
    • Performs a bounded read of the input stream up to @bytesize_limit + 2 bytes (preserving Rack's memory protection semantics).
    • Parses query pairs using a dedicated Rack::QueryParser configured with @bytesize_limit.
    • Pre-populates env["rack.request.form_pairs"] and env["rack.request.form_vars"], preventing downstream middleware or controller parameter parsing from re-evaluating the body against Rack's global 4 MB limit.

  2. Configuration:

    • Adds config.action_mailbox.mailgun_payload_size_limit, defaulting to 25.megabytes.
    • Inserts the middleware via insert_after Rack::Runtime, which:
      • Safely precedes Rack::MethodOverride in standard applications.
      • Operates cleanly in API-only applications (config.api_only = true) where Rack::Runtime is present.
      • Preserves default middleware order, unshift semantics, and host authorization protection.

  3. Documentation and Tests:

    • Documented config.action_mailbox.mailgun_payload_size_limit in guides/source/configuring.md.
    • Added unit tests for RequestParser verifying bounded reads, limit enforcement, and isolation from unrelated endpoints.
    • Added integration test verifying large Mailgun payloads (> 4 MB) are accepted by the ingress endpoint.
    • Added Railties middleware tests verifying custom limit configuration and API-only boot compatibility.
    • Added CHANGELOG entry in actionmailbox/CHANGELOG.md.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #58732.

The Associations Guide and Active Record documentation explain that build_association returns a new, unsaved object for a has_one association. However, they do not make clear that building this object replaces the association's current target and may immediately modify, nullify, or destroy an existing persisted record.

This behavior is particularly surprising with dependent: :destroy, where calling build_association on a persisted owner destroys the existing target before the newly built object is saved.

Detail

This Pull Request clarifies the has_one saving and replacement behavior in both the Active Record API documentation and the Associations Guide:

  • In activerecord/lib/active_record/associations.rb:
    • Updated the Auto-saving overview to note that replaced objects will still be removed or saved to update foreign keys according to the association's :dependent option.
    • Explicitly documented in build_association that an existing associated record is immediately removed or destroyed according to the :dependent option.
  • In guides/source/association_basics.md:
    • Added a warning callout in section 2.6 clarifying that while the newly built object remains unsaved, building it replaces the current target and immediately removes or destroys any existing persisted target according to :dependent.

items.content_html:
Since #58060, a Ractor built its notifier from a snapshot of the subscriptions taken on first use and never looked at it again, so subscriptions added or removed later were invisible to it. The snapshot was also assembled outside Fanout's mutex.

Replace Fanout's Concurrent::Map / Array pair with Fanout::Registry, which subscribe / unsubscribe replace instead of mutating in place. A Ractor compares identity to tell that the registry it materialized went stale, and adopts the new one.

cc @gmcgibbon @Edouard-chin
items.title: Make notification subscriptions an immutable registry

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #58292.

extract_value_from_default returned actual Ruby true / false objects for DEFAULT TRUE / DEFAULT FALSE literals, unlike every other branch in that method, which returns a String.

This pre-cast value became the attribute's value_before_type_cast, so overriding a boolean column with:

attribute :name, :integer

fed a Ruby boolean directly into Integer#deserialize, raising:

NoMethodError: undefined method `to_i' for true

This is a residual gap in fb04401a66 ("Stop deserializing column defaults"), which fixed the general column-default double-casting issue behind #58292 but reintroduced the same failure specifically for SQLite's TRUE / FALSE literal parsing.

Detail

This Pull Request changes SQLite boolean default extraction to return "1" / "0" strings instead of Ruby true / false objects.

This matches the plain-scalar contract of the other branches in extract_value_from_default and restores the pre-8.1 behavior where the column default round-trips through the overriding type correctly.

Regression coverage verifies that:

  • a boolean schema default can be read through an overridden integer attribute type; and
  • a non-boolean integer value can still be written and reloaded through the overridden attribute.

Additional information

MySQL / Trilogy already return plain numeric strings for tinyint(1) defaults and are unaffected by this regression.

PostgreSQL already returns the literal "true" / "false" string, rather than a cast Ruby Boolean, from its own extract_value_from_default, so it is not affected by this particular regression.

PostgreSQL has separate, longstanding limitations with overriding native boolean columns with non-boolean attribute types. Those behaviors predate this regression and are outside the scope of this change.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Rich text holding a content attachment (<action-text-attachment content-type="text/html" content="…">) can't be rendered from a namespaced controller, from a non-HTML request, or outside a request. ActionText::Attachables::ContentAttachment#to_html hands the ActionText::Content object to the renderer, so Action View resolves it as an object partial:

  • From Admin::MessagesController, prefix_partial_path_with_controller_namespace turns action_text/contents/content into admin/action_text/contents/_content, which doesn't exist: ActionView::MissingTemplate.
  • From a JSON request, the lookup is restricted to formats: [:json], so the HTML partial isn't found either. (Top-level content passes formats: :html explicitly; the nested render doesn't.)
  • From a job, there's no controller renderer, so Action Text falls back to Class.new(ActionController::Base).renderer, whose prefix is nil, and merge_prefix_into_object_path raises undefined method 'include?' for nil.

We hit all three in production this evening: a comment with a content attachment 500'd the create request from a namespaced comments controller and then failed every webhook delivery job for that event.

Detail

Render the content partial by path with formats: :html, the same way ActionText::Content#to_rendered_html_with_layout renders top-level content. Adds tests for the namespaced controller, the JSON request, and the job, each of which raises without the change.

Checklist

  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why.
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.

items.content_html:
This Pull Request adds a fast path for the common configuration, where no acronyms are defined:

  • Downcasing every run of letters and digits and looking each up in an empty acronyms table is exactly String#downcase!, so that is what runs when inflections.acronyms is empty.
  • Capitalizing the first letter with sub!(/\A[[:alpha:]]/) is exactly String#capitalize! when the string is ASCII and everything after the first letter is already lowercase, which is the case without acronyms. ASCII has no titlecase mappings that differ from upcase; ß and the ǆ digraphs do, so non-ASCII results keep the regexp.

With acronyms defined, both regexps run as before, so applications that configure acronyms see no change in behavior or cost.

Additional information

Behavior is unchanged.

Benchmark (Ruby 4.0.6, YJIT enabled, Apple M-series, benchmark-ips with 2s warmup, each case in a fresh process; nanoseconds per call and allocations, before → after):

items.content_html:
Detail

  • TimeWithZone#xmlschema (and its aliases iso8601 and rfc3339) for non-UTC values now converts the UTC time with getlocal(utc_offset) and formats it with Time#iso8601, which already prints a fixed offset as +HH:MM and truncates offsets with seconds to minutes exactly like seconds_to_utc_offset did. The regexp substitution and the format call are gone. Values built from a DateTime (a DateTime local time, or utc computed from one) go through the existing private transfer_time_values_to_utc_constructor first, as initialize already does, since DateTime has no getlocal.
  • TimeWithZone#to_s does the same with Time#to_s, whose %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z output is the format this method was mimicking by hand, including UTC for UTC values.
  • TimeZone.seconds_to_utc_offset interpolates the sign and two-digit hours and minutes from a frozen table instead of calling format with an array. It is called by every formatted_offset in Active Support (Time, DateTime, TimeZone, TimeWithZone), so to_s, inspect, rfc2822, and to_fs(:rfc822) all get the saving.

Additional information

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Callbacks run in the order they are registered, and the ones inherited from a parent class come first. Since the parent class body is evaluated before the subclass body, a base class cannot register a callback that depends on the state its subclasses set up. In a base controller this comes up constantly: authorization, canonical redirects, breadcrumbs, conditional GET support.

prepend has the mirror problem. It puts a callback in front of the callbacks registered so far, which is what a concern needs in order to run before the callbacks it inherits, but it cannot keep it there: the next prepend wins. So a base class cannot reliably register the callback that establishes the context — the current tenant, say — that every other callback, prepended or not, relies on.

Neither end of the chain can be claimed, and the ordering information is already in the chain, so this seems worth having in the framework.

Example 1: a base controller acting on a record its subclasses load

Today, since set_callback removes duplicates, a subclass can re-register the inherited callback to move it after its own. This is the workaround the filter ordering write-up documents, and it does work:

# Today
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  before_action :authorize_record, only: %i[ show edit ]

  private
    def authorize_record
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can?(action_name, @record)
    end
end

class ArticlesController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_record
  # Required, or :authorize_record runs first and @record is nil.
  append_before_action :authorize_record, only: %i[ show edit ]
end

class CommentsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_record
  append_before_action :authorize_record, only: %i[ show edit ] # ... and again
end

The line — conditions included — has to be repeated in every subclass, it silently stops authorizing the moment one of them forgets it, and the base class has no way to enforce it. In the application this patch grew out of, that was 17 of 21 subclasses of one base controller repeating the same callback with the same :if condition. The other approach people reach for is deferring the registration with TracePoint until the subclass body has been evaluated, which is not thread-safe and breaks on anonymous and reopened classes.

# This Pull Request
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  before_action :authorize_record, innermost: true, only: %i[ show edit ]
end

class ArticlesController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_record # runs before :authorize_record
end

Example 2: a base controller establishing the context everything else needs

# Today
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  prepend_before_action :set_current_tenant
end

module Authentication
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    # Needs Current.tenant. Prepending puts it in front of :set_current_tenant,
    # so the tenant is nil. Appending puts it behind callbacks that must not run
    # before authentication. There is no correct place for it.
    prepend_before_action :authenticate
  end
end

Unlike the first example, this one has no workaround at all: whichever callback prepends last wins, so the base controller can only hope that nothing prepends after it.

# This Pull Request
class ApplicationController < ActionController::Base
  before_action :set_current_tenant, outermost: true
end

# The concern keeps working the way it was written, no matter which controller
# includes it or in which order: :authenticate is prepended in front of every
# regular callback, and still runs after :set_current_tenant.

Detail

ActiveSupport::Callbacks::ClassMethods#set_callback accepts two new options. Think of the chain as a set of layers wrapped around the event: innermost: true keeps the callback closest to it, so every callback that is not itself innermost — including the ones registered later on by subclasses — wraps it. outermost: true keeps it furthest from it, so every callback that is not itself outermost is wrapped by it.

They are named after the nesting rather than after the position in the chain, which keeps them accurate for every kind of callback: an innermost before callback runs after the regular ones, an innermost around callback is wrapped by them, and, since after callbacks run in reverse order, an innermost after callback runs before them. first/last would have been shorter and closer to prepend/append, but would have read backwards for after.

The options only say which end of the chain a callback belongs to, they do not make it unique, and they compose with prepend rather than override it: within its end, a callback is appended, or prepended when prepend: true is given. This is what the after_* callbacks defined by define_model_callbacks rely on to run in declaration order. A subclass registering its own pinned callback lands after the one of its parent, just like any callback registered later, so at the outermost end the parent's stays the first to run and at the innermost end the subclass's becomes the last to run. Asking for both ends at once raises an ArgumentError.

The options work wherever Active Support callbacks do. ActiveModel::Callbacks had to be taught to accept them, since define_model_callbacks validates its option keys; Active Job and Action Mailer pass them through already.

Implementation

The chain is ordered from the outermost callback to the innermost one, and is now read as three partitions: the outermost callbacks, the regular ones, and the innermost ones. A callback is inserted at the inside end of its own partition, or at the outside end of it when prepended, which is the whole of it:

def insertion_index(callback, prepend)
  if callback.outermost?
    prepend ? 0 : @chain.count(&:outermost?)
  elsif callback.innermost?
    prepend ? first_innermost_index : @chain.length
  else
    prepend ? @chain.count(&:outermost?) : first_innermost_index
  end
end

The partition a callback belongs to is recorded on the Callback itself, so the chain stays a single list and skip_callback, reset_callbacks, and the duplicate removal performed by set_callback keep working on it unchanged. merge_conditional_options carries the flags over, so a conditionally skipped callback keeps its place. With no pinned callback in a chain, both branches reduce to the previous push and unshift, so existing chains are unaffected.

The innermost_*_action and outermost_*_action callbacks are optional

AbstractController::Callbacks additionally defines innermost_before_action, innermost_around_action, innermost_after_action, and their outermost_* counterparts. They are only shorthands for the options, added for symmetry with prepend_before_action; the options are the API, and are what the guides lead with.

If growing the public surface of AbstractController::Callbacks by six methods is not wanted, they can be dropped from this Pull Request without touching anything else — the feature is fully usable through the options, and the tests cover both forms and assert that they produce identical chains.

Additional information

Beyond the tests in the diff, the following was verified while writing this and is not part of the commit:

  • Randomized differential test against the previous behavior. 200 iterations of random set_callback calls with and without :prepend, interleaved with skip_callback, compared against a reference model implementing the old push/unshift/delete semantics. Zero divergence for chains that use neither option, which is the backward-compatibility claim.
  • Randomized check of the partition invariant. insertion_index assumes the chain is always [outermost*, regular*, innermost*]. 300 runs over a three-level inheritance hierarchy with mixed :before/:after/:around, random pin flags, random :prepend and interleaved skip_callback never broke it.
  • Every behavioral claim in the documentation was executed. A script asserts the twelve statements made in the RDoc, the guides, and the CHANGELOGs against real callback chains, including the ones about after callbacks running in reverse order and about where a subclass's pinned callback lands. Two claims were wrong when first written and were corrected this way.
  • Mutation test on merge_conditional_options. Removing the propagation of the flags there makes test_conditionally_skipping_an_innermost_callback_keeps_it_innermost fail, which confirms that test actually covers the path.
  • A local run of GitHub Copilot's reviewer and a security review found, respectively, three documentation defects (since fixed) and no security findings; notably, no callback registered by the framework itself uses either option, so no existing chain changes.

The test suites were run on Ruby 3.4.1 and 4.0.5, including the Ractor tests that only run on 4.0: activesupport/test/callbacks_test.rb, actionpack/test/controller/filters_test.rb, actionpack/test/abstract/callbacks_test.rb, activemodel/test/cases/callbacks_test.rb, activemodel/test/cases/validations/callbacks_test.rb and actionmailer/test/callbacks_test.rb.

items.content_html:
Following on from ruby/ruby#18647

String#tr!now accepts a Hash, which substitutes in one pass over the UTF-8 string with no Regexp and no round-trip.

tr! raises on invalid encodings, so the fast path is guarded on valid_encoding? and falls back to gsub!.

Both encoders are updated, though JSONGemCoderEncoder is the one installed by default whenever JSON::Coder is available.

The escape step in isolation. tr! builds a translation table per call, so its slower on pre-compiled Regexp for documents under 128 bytes with nothing to escape and is faster everywhere else:

small: 48 bytes
ruby 4.1.0dev (2026-09-11T11:29:25Z master d6b4cbbbb1) +PRISM [arm64-darwin25]
Warming up --------------------------------------
               gsub!   619.603k i/100ms
                 tr!   459.017k i/100ms
Calculating -------------------------------------
               gsub!      6.181M (± 2.7%) i/s  (161.79 ns/i) -     30.980M in   5.012225s
                 tr!      4.512M (± 1.7%) i/s  (221.63 ns/i) -     22.951M in   5.086542s

Comparison:
gsub!:  6180917.7 i/s
  tr!:  4512073.2 i/s - 1.37x  slower

large html: 51300 bytes
ruby 4.1.0dev (2026-09-11T11:29:25Z master d6b4cbbbb1) +PRISM [arm64-darwin25]
Warming up --------------------------------------
               gsub!   191.000 i/100ms
                 tr!     2.010k i/100ms
Calculating -------------------------------------
               gsub!      1.954k (± 1.3%) i/s  (511.68 μs/i) -      9.932k in   5.082055s
                 tr!     20.452k (± 1.0%) i/s   (48.89 μs/i) -    102.510k in   5.012214s

Comparison:
gsub!:     1954.3 i/s
  tr!:    20452.0 i/s - 10.47x  faster

require "benchmark/ips"

UTF8 = Encoding.find("UTF-8")
BINARY = Encoding.find("ASCII-8BIT")

ESCAPES = {
  "\u2028" => '\u2028', "\u2029" => '\u2029',
  ">" => '\u003e', "<" => '\u003c', "&" => '\u0026',
}
BYTES = ESCAPES.to_h { |k, v| [k.b, v.b] }
REGEX = Regexp.union(*BYTES.keys)

def escape_gsub(json)
  json.force_encoding(BINARY)
  json.gsub!(REGEX, BYTES)
  json.force_encoding(UTF8)
end

def escape_tr(json)
  return escape_gsub(json) unless json.valid_encoding?
  json.tr!(ESCAPES)
  json
end

CLEAN = %({"id":1,"title":"a perfectly ordinary document"})
HTML = %({"id":1,"title":"a <b>perfectly</b> ordinary & document"})

{ "small" => CLEAN, "large html" => HTML * 900 }.each do |name, src|
  raise "paths disagree" unless escape_gsub(src.dup).b == escape_tr(src.dup).b
  puts "#{name}: #{src.bytesize} bytes"

  Benchmark.ips do |x|
    x.report("gsub!") { escape_gsub(src.dup) }
    x.report("tr!") { escape_tr(src.dup) }
    x.compare!(order: :baseline)
  end
end

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

The motivation started with the fast_blank C extension that is still in use in some production applications.

Unfortunately, even with YJIT, it is still faster than AS#blank? today.

So I decided to figure out a way to port it to plain Ruby or do a rewrite that would allow us to use plain Ruby and YJIT to match its speed.

Detail

This Pull Request changes String#blank? to scan bytes instead of running the regexp for the strings that make up virtually all real input:

  • ASCII-only strings in any encoding, and valid UTF-8 strings, go through a private utf8_blank? byte loop. It accepts the six ASCII whitespace bytes and the UTF-8 byte sequences of the other 19 codepoints that [[:space:]] matches (U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000..U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000), decoding each multi-byte sequence to its codepoint so the constants in the code are the codepoints themselves.
  • Every other string keeps using the regexp: strings in UTF-16/32 or legacy encodings, and invalid byte sequences (so they keep raising ArgumentError). This is deliberate. Onigmo's [[:space:]] uses a per-encoding table for legacy encodings (KOI8-R treats 0x9A as whitespace, ISO-8859-1 treats 0xA0 as whitespace but 0x85 not, TIS-620 treats 0xA0 as whitespace), and the regexp is the only primitive in Ruby that consults those tables. fast_blank's blank_as? gets 57 legacy encodings wrong for exactly this reason.
  • The loop lives in a private helper so that blank? itself has no local variables. YJIT initializes every local on method entry, and with the loop inline the empty string measured 6 percent slower than before; with the helper it is identical.

String::BLANK_RE and String::ENCODED_BLANKS are unchanged and still used for the regexp path.

Additional information

Benchmark (Ruby 4.0.6, YJIT enabled, Apple M-series, benchmark-ips with 2s warmup; million iterations per second; allocations per call are zero for all three columns on every row):

input before after x fast_blank (C) x
nil 446.9 449.9 1.01x 449.7 1.01x
"" 147.6 147.0 1.00x 139.5 0.95x
"a" 8.7 61.3 7.09x 88.9 10.29x
"this is a test" 16.2 61.3 3.79x 89.0 5.51x
"\n" 10.2 61.1 5.97x 88.7 8.67x
" " 16.6 49.1 2.95x 55.2 3.32x
" this is a longer test" 14.0 52.3 3.73x 68.0 4.85x
U+00A0 (no-break space) only 18.2 36.4 2.00x 84.3 4.63x
Cyrillic text 17.8 41.6 2.34x 84.2 4.73x
space + Cyrillic text 12.7 37.7 2.98x 62.7 4.95x
hiragana 17.4 30.0 1.72x 78.1 4.49x
emoji 17.3 41.6 2.40x 74.5 4.30x
136 spaces 1.24 2.68 2.16x 1.16 0.94x
1000 x's 16.2 61.3 3.78x 86.5 5.33x
ISO-8859-1 "\xA0" 10.4 9.3 0.89x 91.4 8.83x

The last row is the one input class that gets slightly slower: a string in a legacy encoding that contains non-ASCII bytes pays about 10ns for the encoding check before reaching the regexp. Ruby 3.3 and 3.4 with YJIT also inline getbyte, and the byte loop beats the regexp there as well.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

The Associations Guide explains that build_association returns a new, unsaved object for a has_one association. However, it does not make clear that building this object replaces the association's current target and may immediately modify or destroy the existing persisted record.

This behavior is particularly surprising with dependent: :destroy, where calling build_association destroys the existing target before the newly built object is saved.

Related to #58732.

Detail

This Pull Request adds a warning to the has_one saving behavior documentation clarifying that:

  • the object returned by build_association remains unsaved;
  • building it replaces the current association target; and
  • Rails immediately removes a persisted target according to the association's :dependent option, including destroying it when dependent: :destroy is configured.

This is a documentation-only change and does not alter the existing Active Record behavior.

Additional information

No tests or CHANGELOG entry are needed because this change only clarifies existing documented behavior.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #58736. Ruby master prevents a worker Ractor from compiling a previously unseen non-strict template into a view context class that the main Ractor owns. That raises Ractor::IsolationError in the actual Action View rendering path.

Detail

Give Action View each worker Ractor its own empty-template-cache view context class. Controller-specific view context classes are also cached per Ractor, so their compiled method containers remain owned by the Ractor that performs template compilation.

The resolver regression now renders through a real Action View class created from a main-Ractor-owned frozen FileSystemResolver. It passes explicit frozen lookup details inside the worker to avoid unrelated I18n Ractor state.

Additional information

Manual validation on Ruby master:

  • Reproduced the reported isolation failure with the original test-only approach.
  • Ran a standalone render through a frozen FileSystemResolver and real Action View worker-Ractor class; it rendered "hello" and compiled into the worker-owned class.
  • Ran the two affected template test files 20 times in fresh processes without a failure.
  • Ran the targeted two-file Action View test command successfully: 58 runs, 176 assertions.
  • Ran the full Action View suite successfully: 3,292 runs, 7,449 assertions.
  • Ran RuboCop on all four changed files with no offenses.

Checklist

  • This Pull Request is related to one change.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why, including the related issue.
  • Tests are updated for the Ruby master regression.
  • CHANGELOG files are not needed for this minor compatibility bug fix.
items.title: Fix #58736: make Action View template compilation Ractor-local
